tone_statements.quote: Tone in Syer and Supyire is marked on every vowel as follows: the acute accent is used to mark High tone, grave accent to mark Low tone. Absence of a tone on a vowel corresponds to Mid tone. Contour tones on short vowels are marked as a combination of register tones: a haček stands for a LH (ǎ), a circumflex for a HL (â), the grave accent + hyphen for Low-Mid (a᷅), and on long vowels by L on the first vowel and Ø on the second (àa). [...] The realization of the conditional in intransitive clauses for all three tonal classes of verbs is illustrated in (18).

sources.note: pp. 287-288: the grammar's Phonology chapter 'is thus essentially about segmental phonology, with little attention to suprasegmentals and prosody except for a tantalizingly brief and undeveloped reference to syllable stress (16). sources.note: Silent on stress/accent. The phonology sketch covers vowels, semi-vowels, consonants and '4. Les tons' only: 'Notre enquête a été beaucoup trop rapide pour nous permettre l'étude tonétique de la langue. Il appert néanmoins que dans la 3e classe, les mots terminés en l forment leur pluriel par un tonème.. Nous ne donnons que le ton « relatif »' (p. 216). No word 'accent' anywhere in the scanned pages.

sources.note: By the grammar's author: Syer transcription distinguishes three register tones High (acute), Mid (unmarked) and Low (grave), with contour tones LH, HL and Low-Mid on short vowels and L+unmarked on long vowels (fn. 6); verbs fall into three tonal classes M, HL and L, the L class being 'the most stable' (para <18>, table (18)); tone is grammatical: some TAM values are marked only by the tone of the subject pronoun and the tonal shape of the verb (remote past = L subject pronoun, para <3>), the conditional = L subject pronoun + auxiliary mɛ + a HL tune whose placement depends on object presence…
